analysis.one_liner: Lets people sue federal officers for money damages when they violate constitutional rights.
analysis.headline: The bill, which would let people harmed by federal officials sue them for damages, was introduced in August 2024 with 12 House sponsors and never received a committee hearing or a vote before Congress ended.
analysis.plain_summary: Today, people injured by federal agents, like border patrol or immigration officers, generally cannot sue those officers for money damages, because the Supreme Court has limited the judge-made 'Bivens' remedy to a narrow set of cases. This bill writes that remedy into law by amending the federal civil rights statute (42 U.S.C. 1983) to cover people acting under U.S. as well as state authority. It was referred to the House Judiciary Committee and died there without a hearing or vote.
analysis.who_benefits: People whose constitutional rights are violated by federal officials, such as people mistreated by border patrol, immigration, or other federal law enforcement officers, would gain a way to recover money damages in court.

how_it_helps.text: The bill amends the civil rights statute that currently lets people sue state and local officials who violate constitutional rights, so it also covers anyone acting under authority of the United States.

This would restore in statute the damages remedy the Supreme Court created in Bivens v. Six Unknown Named Agents (1971) and has since narrowed in cases like Ziglar v. Abbasi and Egbert v. Boule, leaving many victims of federal officers without any compensation.
The bill was introduced by Rep. Hank Johnson with 11 Democratic cosponsors and referred to the House Judiciary Committee.

analysis.who_pays: Federal officials and agencies would face personal and institutional liability for damages; the Justice Department typically indemnifies federal employees, so much of the cost could fall on taxpayers, and agents could face the deterrent of personal suits.

drawbacks.text: Critics of reviving Bivens argue that damages suits against federal officers could chill law enforcement and that Congress should weigh 'special factors' like national security before creating liability, a concern the Supreme Court has repeatedly cited.
Because federal employees are generally represented and indemnified by the government, damage awards and defense costs could ultimately be paid by taxpayers rather than the individual officers.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The bill addresses a real gap: a person beaten or wrongfully detained by a federal agent often has no federal damages remedy at all, while a person harmed by a local police officer can sue. The cost is expanded liability for federal agencies and possible defensive behavior by agents; how large that cost is depends on views about whether damages suits deter misconduct or deter legitimate policing. The bill was a one-sentence amendment piggybacking on an existing statute, so its design was simple, but it got no committee consideration where such questions could be examined.

outcome.mechanism: It was referred to the House Judiciary Committee in August 2024, four months before the session ended, and the committee never took it up, so it died when the Congress ended.

narrative.text: The Bivens Act was introduced in the House on August 2, 2024, by Rep. Hank Johnson of Georgia with 11 Democratic cosponsors.
The same day, it was referred to the House Committee on the Judiciary; no further action appears in the record.
The Congress ended on January 3, 2025, without the bill receiving a hearing, markup, or floor vote.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Federal officers and agencies remain largely shielded from personal damages suits for constitutional violations, so people harmed by federal agents are still left without a remedy in most cases.

for.name: Rep. Hank C. 'Hank' Johnson
for.what_they_did: Introduced the Bivens Act to create a damages remedy against federal officials and referred it to the Judiciary Committee.

for.name: 11 of 216 House Democrats
for.what_they_did: Cosponsored the bill; no Republican cosponsored it.

against.name: House Judiciary Committee leadership
against.role: Chair of the committee where the bill sat
against.what_they_did: Never scheduled the bill for a hearing or markup after its referral in August 2024; the committee took no action before the Congress ended.

sides.party_line_note: All 12 sponsors and cosponsors were House Democrats; no Republican signed on, and the Republican-controlled committee never acted on it.

industries.industry: Federal law enforcement agencies (Border Patrol, ICE, FBI, etc.)
industries.note: The bill would expose federal officers and their agencies to money-damage suits for constitutional violations, ending the practical shield they now enjoy in most cases. It matters to ordinary people because it is the difference between having a remedy when a federal agent causes harm and having none.

industries.industry: Federal taxpayers (through DOJ indemnification of employees)
industries.note: Because the government typically pays judgments and legal defense for federal employees sued for official acts, expanded liability would be financed largely by taxpayers.
